Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, Marshall Plan figures

source: original; stimulus table from U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, Marshall Plan figures (approximate)

stimulus.source_note: Aid figures: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian, Marshall Plan figures (approximate, rounded to one decimal place).
stimulus.text:
Marshall Plan aid, 1948-1952 (billions of dollars, rounded)

| Country | Aid received |
| United Kingdom | 3.3 |
| France | 2.7 |
| Italy | 1.5 |
| West Germany | 1.4 |
| Netherlands | 1.1 |
| All other recipients | 3.3 |
| Total | about 13 |

stem: The pattern of aid in the table best supports which conclusion about the Marshall Plan?

options.text: Aid went mostly to Eastern Europe, where Communist governments ruled
options.misconception: Background from the books: the plan aided Western Europe; the Soviet Union kept Eastern Europe out of it.

options.text: Aid was spread evenly among all the countries of Europe
options.misconception: The table shows wide differences, from 3.3 billion dollars for the United Kingdom to 1.1 billion for the Netherlands.

options.text: Aid went only to countries that had fought on the Axis side in the war
options.misconception: Background from the books: Britain and France, both Allies, received the two largest shares.

options.text: Aid went mainly to the largest economies of Western Europe

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Marshall Plan aided Western Europe, and the Soviet Union barred Eastern Europe from taking part.
rationales.B: The table shows uneven amounts, from 3.3 billion dollars down to 1.1 billion, not an even spread.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Britain and France were Allies, and they received the two largest shares in the table.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the largest shares went to Britain, France, Italy, and West Germany, the biggest Western European economies, to rebuild them.
rationales.general:
1. The two largest shares go to the United Kingdom and France, then Italy and West Germany.
2. Background from the books: those four were the largest economies of Western Europe.
3. Background from the books: the smallest listed share goes to the Netherlands, a smaller economy.
4. The money therefore followed economic size in Western Europe, not an even spread.
Remember: when a table ranks recipients, ask what the top recipients have in common.
